title: Best AI Music Theory Tools 2026: 20 Tutors and Ear Trainers
summary: Learn music theory with AI in 2026: 20 tools compared, from ChatGPT and Hookpad to EarMaster and ToneGym. Free plans and prices checked in November 2026.
body_markdown:
**The best AI music theory tools in 2026 split into two jobs: tools that explain and tools that check.** Chat tutors such as ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini explain a concept in plain words, at any hour, at any level. Drill apps such as EarMaster, ToneGym, and musictheory.net check whether you actually learned it, by ear and on the staff. You need one of each, because research shows chat models still guess on multi-step music reasoning. Below are 20 tools in seven groups, with free plans and prices checked on November 7, 2026, and the ChatGPT prices and the Chordify free plan re-checked on November 12, 2026.


The need is old. Around the year 1030, an Italian monk named Guido of Arezzo had a problem every music teacher still has: students forget. His answer was the syllables ut, re, mi, fa, sol, la, and, in the generations after him, a diagram drawn on the palm of the hand. A singer pointed to a knuckle and sang the note it stood for. The hand was a tutor that went everywhere and never got tired.


*Cover image: a Guidonian hand from a late 15th-century manuscript. Wikimedia Commons, public domain.*


> **TL;DR:** We compared **20 AI music theory tools** by the job they do: chat tutors that explain (ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini), ear trainers that test (EarMaster, ToneGym), chord tools that suggest (Hookpad with Aria, ChordChord), and practice apps that listen (Yousician, Skoove). Free plans checked November 2026. Start with the[music theory AI](https://www.taskade.com/agents/education/music-theory-tutor) tutor agent.


---

For proving you learned it, a drill site or ear trainer grades every answer. For writing songs, a chord tool puts theory on screen while you work. For playing, an app that listens corrects your notes and timing.

## What Is an AI Music Theory Tool?


**An AI music theory tool uses machine learning to explain, test, or apply the rules of harmony, rhythm, melody, and notation.** In 2026 the term covers six kinds of products: chat tutors, theory courses with drills, ear trainers, chord and song-analysis tools, instrument apps that listen, and notation software. Only some of them use AI. The rest use fixed rules, and that is a feature, because fixed rules make a reliable checker.


Each group hands you something different at the end of a practice session:


```text
WHAT YOU GET BACK                  EXAMPLE TOOLS                       DOES IT CHECK YOU?
────────────────────────────────   ─────────────────────────────────   ──────────────────
An explanation in plain words      ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, Taskade    Only if you ask
A lesson plus graded drills        musictheory.net, Musicca            Yes, every answer
A score on what you heard          EarMaster, ToneGym, Perfect Ear     Yes, by ear
Chord ideas that fit a key         Hookpad + Aria, ChordChord          No, you judge
The chords of a real song          Chordify, Moises                    No, you play along
Feedback on what you played        Yousician, Simply Piano, Skoove     Yes, it listens
A score you can print and play     MuseScore Studio                    Playback only


```


Which groups actually use AI? On the pages we read on November 7, 2026, musictheory.net, Musicca, and MuseScore Studio make no AI claim. EarMaster describes an "intelligent questioning engine" that adapts exercises to your performance, and ToneGym says its games "adapt to your level," without calling either one AI. Hookpad's Aria, ChordChord, LANDR Composer, Moises, and the chat tutors describe themselves as AI. The rule-based tools stay on this list because a chat tutor needs something that checks it.


There is also a seventh shape, which is where Taskade fits: a tutor you build and keep, connected to your own lesson list and practice log, so the explanations follow a plan instead of starting from zero each time.

## Can AI Actually Teach Music Theory? What the Research Says


**AI chat tutors are good at explaining music theory and weak at multi-step music reasoning.** On MusicTheoryBench, a college-level test of 372 multiple-choice questions, GPT-4 scored 58.2% on music knowledge and 25.6% on music reasoning with no examples, where random guessing scores 25%. Better prompts raised both scores, but reasoning stayed far below knowledge.


MusicTheoryBench comes from the ChatMusician paper (Yuan et al., arXiv 2402.16153, February 2024, published in ACL 2024 Findings). A professional college music teacher wrote the questions from college-level textbooks and exam papers, and a team of musicians reviewed them over several rounds. The benchmark holds 269 knowledge questions, 98 reasoning questions, and 5 questions kept aside as few-shot examples. Every question has four options, so a random guess lands at 25%.


Setup (GPT-4, 2024) Music knowledge Music reasoning


Random guess 25.0% 25.0%


Zero-shot 58.2% 25.6%


Zero-shot plus 5 worked examples 64.1% 38.0%


Role-play prompt 68.3% 36.6%


Role-play plus 5 worked examples (best reasoning) 68.8% 39.5%


Chain-of-thought 68.4% 36.7%


Chain-of-thought plus 5 worked examples 69.9% 34.9%


*Source: Table 3, "ChatMusician: Understanding and Generating Music Intrinsically with LLM," arXiv 2402.16153, read November 7, 2026.*


A second study points the same way, with a twist. In "Teaching LLMs Music Theory with In-Context Learning and Chain-of-Thought Prompting" (Pond and Fujinaga, arXiv 2503.22853, March 2025), the authors tested ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini on questions from an official Royal Conservatory of Music Level 6 exam: intervals, chords, keys, cadences, and meter. They fed the music in four text formats (ABC, Humdrum, MEI, and MusicXML), with and without teaching prompts. Without context, the best result was ChatGPT with MEI at 52%. With context, the best was Claude with MEI at 75%.


Study Models tested Best result What it teaches a learner


MusicTheoryBench (Feb 2024) GPT-4, GPT-3.5, open models 39.5% on reasoning with role-play and examples Explanations are strong, multi-step logic is weak


RCM Level 6 study (Mar 2025) ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini 75% with teaching prompts (Claude, MEI) The format of the notes and the prompt change the score


Two honest caveats. Both studies tested models from 2024 and early 2025, and newer models can score higher. We found no independent re-run of MusicTheoryBench on the consumer chat apps of late 2026, so we do not quote a 2026 score. The second caveat is on the tutor side: a chat app cannot hear you play in a text chat, and LANDR's own blog notes that chatbots "sometimes hallucinate and essentially make up false advice."


> **Citation capsule:** In the 2024 MusicTheoryBench study, GPT-4 answered 58.2% of music knowledge questions correctly but only 25.6% of music reasoning questions, near the 25% random baseline. A 2025 study reached 75% on a conservatory exam only with careful teaching prompts. Chat tutors explain theory well. Check their answers in a drill app or by ear.


The practical rules that follow from the research:


- **Ask for note names, not only Roman numerals.** "Dm7, G7, Cmaj7" is easy to check on a keyboard. "ii-V-I" alone is not.
- **Paste notes in one text format.** ABC notation or a plain list such as "C E G B" works better than a description of a picture.
- **Ask the tutor to count half steps.** A wrong count shows up at once.
- **Check each answer in a drill app or on an instrument.** That is the job of the "check" tools in this list.

## AI Chat Tutors


Chat tutors explain. They answer "why" questions at any level, rephrase until a concept clicks, and write practice quizzes on demand. They do not hear you, and they need a checker. For a narrower helper focused on assignments, see the[music homework helper](https://www.taskade.com/agents/education/music-homework-helper) agent.


### 1.[ChatGPT](https://chatgpt.com/) : Best Free Tutor for Everyday Theory Questions


[ChatGPT](https://chatgpt.com/) is OpenAI's general assistant, and for most learners it is the first music theory tutor they try. Ask why a dominant seventh wants to resolve or how modes relate to the major scale, and you get a clear answer at your level.


**Key features:** text and voice chat; file and image uploads, so you can share a photo of a worksheet; quizzes and flashcards on request.


**Free plan (checked Nov 7, 2026):** the pricing page lists "Unlimited text chats," with "Limited messages with uploads," "Limited voice chats," and "Limited memory and context" on Free.


**Pros:**


- Explains at any level, from first notes to advanced harmony
- Voice chat turns it into a spoken quiz partner while your hands are on an instrument


**Cons:**


- Multi-step harmony analysis can go wrong without a visible error (see the research section)
- It cannot hear you play in a text chat


**Pricing:** the pricing page lists Go at $8 a month, Plus at $20 a month, and Pro from $100 a month in the US (checked 2026-11-12).


**Bottom line:** the easiest free place to ask a theory question, as long as you check the answer.


### 2.[Claude](https://claude.com/) : Best for Long, Structured Lessons


[Claude](https://claude.com/) is Anthropic's assistant. It tends to write long, well-ordered explanations, which suits a learner who wants a full lesson rather than a one-line answer. Its Artifacts feature can turn a request into a small interactive page, such as an interval quiz you can reuse.


**Key features:** long-form explanations and lesson plans; Artifacts for small interactive drills and reference sheets; memory across conversations; web search and file creation.


**Free plan (checked Nov 7, 2026):** $0 with "Limited usage every 5 hours and every week," "Create Artifacts," and "Memory across conversations." How fast you hit the limit depends on the model, chat length, and file size.


**Pros:**


- Strong at structured, step-by-step lessons
- Artifacts let you keep a drill page instead of a chat transcript
- Scored the best result in the 2025 conservatory-exam study when given teaching prompts


**Cons:**


- Usage caps on Free can cut a long session short
- The same reasoning limits as every chat model apply


**Pricing:** Pro $17/month billed annually ($200 a year) or $20 billed monthly. Max from $100/month.


**Bottom line:** the best chat tutor for a learner who wants a full lesson and a reusable drill.


### 3.[Gemini](https://gemini.google/) : Best Free Option on Google's Stack


[Gemini](https://gemini.google/) is Google's assistant, and its free plan is broad. For a music learner, two features stand out: Gems, which save a custom tutor persona you can return to, and Gemini Live, which turns a theory review into a spoken conversation.


**Key features:** Gems for a saved tutor with your instructions; Gemini Live for voice quizzes; Canvas for drafting worksheets; Deep Research for longer reading on a topic such as the history of tuning systems.


**Free plan (checked Nov 7, 2026):** $0 with a Google Account. The free plan lists Canvas, Gems, Gemini Live, Deep Research, and image generation, plus 15 GB of storage across Google services.


**Pros:**


- A saved Gem keeps your tutor's rules between sessions
- Spoken quizzes work well during practice
- A low-cost first paid tier


**Cons:**


- Free usage limits apply
- The same multi-step reasoning limits as other chat models


**Pricing:** Google AI Plus $4.99/month, Google AI Pro $19.99/month, Google AI Ultra from $99.99/month (US).


**Bottom line:** the natural pick if you already live in Google's apps and want a saved tutor persona for free.

## Free Theory Courses and Drills


These tools check you. They make no AI claim, and that is why they belong here: every answer is graded by fixed rules, so they are the most reliable way to test what a chat tutor taught you.


### 4.[musictheory.net](https://www.musictheory.net/) : Best Free Lessons and Exercises


[musictheory.net](https://www.musictheory.net/) has taught theory on the web for years with short, illustrated lessons and configurable exercises. The interval, note, key-signature, and chord drills grade each answer and keep a running score.


The musictheory.net interval exercise, captured November 2026.


**Key features:** step-by-step lessons from the staff to chord progressions; customizable exercises for notes, intervals, keys, scales, and chords; ear-training exercises.


**Free plan (checked Nov 7, 2026):** the FAQ states that "all content on the site is available free of charge and without ads." The site is supported by its apps.


**Pros:**


- Completely free, no account needed
- Each exercise can be customized to the exact range you are working on
- The cleanest free checker for any chat tutor answer


**Cons:**


- No AI explanations, so a wrong answer gets a mark, not a lesson
- The design is spare compared with game-style apps


**Pricing:** free on the web. The Tenuto app is $4.99 on the App Store (seller musictheory.net, LLC).


**Bottom line:** the free drill site to keep open beside any AI tutor.


### 5.[Musicca](https://www.musicca.com/) : Best Free Toolbox


[Musicca](https://www.musicca.com/) combines lessons, exercises, and a large set of interactive tools. The circle of fifths, chord finder, interval finder, and staff paper make it a useful reference while you study with an AI tutor.


**Key features:** exercises for notes, rhythms, intervals, chords, scales, and key signatures; a chord player, metronome, tuner, note finder, scale finder, circle of fifths, and staff paper; a section for schools.


**Free plan (checked Nov 7, 2026):** the homepage promises "For free, forever." A free account lets you "access all content and remove ads."


**Pros:**


- The widest free tool set in this list
- A free account removes ads and unlocks all content
- Teachers can use it with a class at no cost


**Cons:**


- No adaptive learning path
- No AI explanations


**Pricing:** free. No paid plan is published.


**Bottom line:** the best free reference shelf for checking keys, chords, and intervals as you learn.

## Ear Trainers


Ear trainers check what you hear, which no chat tutor can do in text. Most adapt the difficulty to your results.


### 6.[EarMaster](https://www.earmaster.com/) : Best for Structured Ear Training and Sight-Singing


[EarMaster](https://www.earmaster.com/) is the most complete ear-training curriculum in this list, from first intervals to jazz chord progressions and singing. Its homepage describes "Smart Adaptive Learning," with an "intelligent questioning engine" that adapts exercises to your performance.


**Key features:** a Beginner's Course; general and jazz workshops on intervals, chords, and progressions; interval singing and a Vocal Trainer; customizable drills; a Cloud edition for classrooms and institutions.


**Free plan (checked Nov 7, 2026):** the download page lists "100% free exercises": the first 4 modules of the Beginner's Course, interval and chord identification in Customized Exercise mode, the "Call of the Notes" course, and two song lessons.


**Pros:**


- The deepest curriculum in the group
- Runs on Windows, macOS, iOS, and Android
- A school edition for teachers


**Cons:**


- The website does not publish the all-access subscription price
- A lot of material for a casual learner


**Pricing:** on iOS, content unlocks in packs from $0.99 to $14.99. The desktop all-access subscription and licenses are not priced on the pages we read.


**Bottom line:** the ear trainer to choose if you want a full course, not just a game.


### 7.[ToneGym](https://www.tonegym.co/) : Best Game-Style Ear Workouts


[ToneGym](https://www.tonegym.co/) turns ear training into short games and daily workouts. Its FAQ says each game has "multiple difficulty levels that adapt to your skill" and cites "a global community of 400,000+ musicians" (vendor claim).


**Key features:** ear-training games for intervals, chords, and pitch; daily workouts; statistics; interactive tools; a personalized practice plan on Pro.


**Free plan (checked Nov 7, 2026):** "Free to start, with a Pro plan for full access." Free includes the Music Theory 101 course.


**Pros:**


- Short sessions that fit a busy day
- Adaptive difficulty keeps the next question at the right level


**Cons:**


- Most games sit behind Pro
- No prices on the website itself


**Pricing:** the US App Store lists ToneGym Pro at $13.95/month or $74.99/year. The website also mentions a lifetime option without a price.


**Bottom line:** the most fun way to keep a daily ear-training streak.


### 8.[Perfect Ear](https://perfectear.app/) : Best Low-Cost Mobile Ear Trainer


[Perfect Ear](https://perfectear.app/) , from Crazy Ootka Software AB, is a mobile app for intervals, chords, scales, rhythm, singing, and sight reading. It sells content in small one-time packs instead of a subscription.


**Key features:** interval comparison and identification; chord recognition, inversions, and progressions; rhythm reading and tapping; scale identification; singing exercises; a custom exercise editor.


**Free plan (checked Nov 7, 2026):** free download on iOS and Android, with optional packs.


**Pros:**


- One-time purchases instead of a subscription
- Covers rhythm as well as pitch


**Cons:**


- No AI explanations, so a missed answer gets a mark, not a reason
- Mobile only, with no desktop version for practice at a computer


**Pricing:** US App Store packs from $0.99 (chords, scales, rhythm, intervals), the Full Exercise Pack at $4.99, and Perfect Ear Premium at $14.99.


**Bottom line:** the cheapest way to own a complete mobile ear trainer. Buy the packs for the skills you are drilling this month, and skip the rest until you need them.


### 9.[Functional Ear Trainer](https://www.miles.be/) : Best Free Method for Hearing Notes in a Key


[Functional Ear Trainer](https://www.miles.be/) teaches one idea well: hear each note in relation to the key. Instead of memorizing intervals in isolation, you learn how each scale degree feels against the tonic, which is how most musicians actually hear melodies.


**Key features:** a short cadence sets the key, then you name a single note by its place in that key; you start with a few notes and add more as you improve.


**Free plan (checked Nov 7, 2026):** the official site calls it "THE freeware ear training tool to improve your musical ear."


**Pros:**


- Free, with a method that is easy to learn
- Builds the skill that transcription and improvising rely on


**Cons:**


- Narrow scope: no chords, rhythm, or notation
- Several apps in the stores use the same name, so download from the official site


**Pricing:** free.


**Bottom line:** the best free drill for learning to hear a melody in a key.

## Chord, Songwriting, and Song-Analysis Tools


These tools apply theory. They suggest chords, find them in recordings, or show the theory behind a song you love.


### 10.[Hookpad with Aria](https://www.hooktheory.com/) : Best AI Chord and Melody Partner for Songwriters


[Hookpad](https://www.hooktheory.com/) is Hooktheory's songwriting app, built around scale degrees and Roman numerals, so theory is on screen while you write. Its Aria add-on is the AI part: "Aria can write chords, melody, or both at the same time."


The Hooktheory homepage, captured November 2026.


**Key features:** a chord palette that shows which chords fit the key; melody and chord entry by scale degree; Aria for AI chord and melody suggestions; TheoryTab, a library of more than 80,000 song analyses (homepage, November 7, 2026).


**Free plan (checked Nov 7, 2026):** $0, "No credit card required." The free plan has one melody voice and does not include exports.


**Pros:**


- The tightest link between songwriting and theory in this list
- TheoryTab shows how real songs work, in the same notation
- A lifetime option for Standard


**Cons:**


- Aria is a separate add-on on top of Standard
- Free is a taster, without exports


**Pricing:** Standard $7.99/month or $199 lifetime. Aria AI +$14.99/month (plus tax where applicable).


**Bottom line:** the best place to learn theory by writing songs, with AI as a co-writer.


### 11.[Chordify](https://chordify.net/) : Best for Learning the Chords of Songs You Love


[Chordify](https://chordify.net/) detects the chords in a song and shows them in sync with the music, for guitar, piano, and ukulele. Theory sticks better when it explains a song you already love.


**Key features:** automatic chord detection; chord diagrams that scroll with the recording; transpose and tempo controls on paid plans; PDF chord sheets and MIDI on paid plans.


**Free plan (checked Nov 12, 2026):** Chordify's "Is Chordify free?" page says you can play along with "2 songs per day" with no sign-up, and 4 songs a day with a free account. Premium removes the daily limit.


**Pros:**


- Connects theory to music you actually listen to
- Works on desktop and mobile


**Cons:**


- Auto-detected chords can be wrong or simplified, so check by ear
- Key and tempo changes sit behind a paid plan


**Pricing:** US App Store subscriptions from $8.00 to $9.00 a month and $42.00 to $54.00 a year.


**Bottom line:** the fastest way to find a song's chords, then ask a tutor why they work.


### 12.[Moises](https://moises.ai/) : Best for Slowing Down, Isolating Parts, and Finding Chords


[Moises](https://moises.ai/) uses AI to separate a recording into stems (vocals, drums, bass, and more), slow it down without changing the pitch, and detect chords. For theory practice, it lets you hear the bass line alone and work out the harmony yourself.


**Key features:** stem separation; speed and pitch change; a Chord Finder.


**Free plan (checked Nov 7, 2026):** "a free tier that provides a limited number of uploads each month, with access to a select set of features." Exact limits sit behind a login.


**Pros:**


- Isolating the bass is the fastest way to hear chord roots
- Useful for transcription practice at any level


**Cons:**


- Exact free limits are not public
- It is a practice tool, not a course


**Pricing:** US App Store: Premium $5.99/month or $39.99/year, Pro $29.99/month.


**Bottom line:** the best ear-training companion for learning from real recordings.


### 13.[ChordChord](https://www.chordchord.com/) : Best Browser Chord Progression Generator


[ChordChord](https://www.chordchord.com/) generates chord progressions in the browser from prompts or settings, with piano and guitar charts. It is a quick way to hear what a progression in a given mood or key sounds like.


**Key features:** AI progression generation; piano roll and chord charts; MIDI, WAV, stem, and PDF export; collaboration with invited editors.


**Free plan (checked Nov 7, 2026):** invited collaborators can "listen and make limited edits with a free account." The pricing page lists no standalone free plan.


**Pros:**


- Fast way to hear many progressions in a key
- Exports are "100 % royalty-free" for commercial use, per the pricing page


**Cons:**


- The trial costs money
- Generated progressions need your ear to pick the good ones


**Pricing:** "30 days of Pro for just $9.99," then $27/month. Pro includes 5,000 prompts per month.

## Interval and Key Cheat Sheet


**Counting half steps is the fastest way to check any AI tutor's answer about intervals, chords, or keys.** One half step is the distance from one key on a piano to the very next key, black or white. If the tutor says C to E♭ is a major third, count: C up to E♭ passes C♯ and D, which is 3 half steps, so it is a minor third.


```text
HALF STEPS   INTERVAL           FROM C
──────────   ────────────────   ──────
0           Perfect unison     C
1           Minor 2nd          D♭
2           Major 2nd          D
3           Minor 3rd          E♭
4           Major 3rd          E
5           Perfect 4th        F
6           Tritone            F♯ / G♭
7           Perfect 5th        G
8           Minor 6th          A♭
9           Major 6th          A
10           Minor 7th          B♭
11           Major 7th          B
12           Octave             C


```


The circle of fifths gives every major key and its relative minor. Each step to the right on the sharp row adds one sharp, and each step on the flat row adds one flat:


```text
ACCIDENTALS   0    1    2    3    4    5    6
SHARP KEYS    C    G    D    A    E    B    F♯
minor         Am   Em   Bm   F♯m  C♯m  G♯m  D♯m
FLAT KEYS     C    F    B♭   E♭   A♭   D♭   G♭
minor         Am   Dm   Gm   Cm   Fm   B♭m  E♭m


```


Two more checks that catch common tutor errors. A major triad stacks 4 half steps then 3 (C, E, G). A minor triad stacks 3 then 4 (C, E♭, G). A dominant seventh adds a minor seventh, 10 half steps above the root (G, B, D, F).

## Prompts That Get Accurate Answers From an AI Music Tutor


**The best prompts for an AI music tutor ask for note names, half-step counts, and a confidence level, because those make errors visible.** Copy these five into any chat tutor. Each one is written so you can check the answer without a teacher in the room.


**1. Explain a progression, then quiz me.**


```text
Explain the ii-V-I progression in C major. Give the chord names, the notes in each chord, and the half steps between the roots. Then quiz me with five questions in other keys. Wait for my answers before you show yours.


```


**2. Analyze a melody in text form.**


```text
Here is a melody in ABC notation: [paste]. Name the key, mark each interval in half steps, and list any note outside the key.


```


**3. Plan ear training.**


```text
Build a 4-week ear-training plan for a beginner guitarist. 15 minutes a day. Use intervals, then triads, then seventh chords. For each day, name one drill I can do in a free ear-training app.


```


**4. Analyze a song's chords.**


```text
Analyze these chords from a song: [paste chord list]. Give Roman numerals in the key you think it is in, and say how sure you are. If two keys are possible, name both and explain the difference.


```


**5. Run a strict exam.**


```text
Act as a strict theory examiner. Give me 10 key-signature questions, one at a time, and keep score. Do not give hints unless I ask.


```


Prompts 1, 2, and 4 ask for half steps or a confidence level. That small change turns a fluent paragraph into something you can verify in ten seconds.

## AI Music Theory FAQ


What is the best AI for music theory in 2026?


It depends on the job. For explanations, ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini all work well on free plans. For checking what you learned, musictheory.net and Musicca are free, and EarMaster is the most complete ear trainer. For songwriting, Hookpad with Aria suggests chords that fit your key. For a tutor that remembers your plan, try the Taskade music theory tutor agent.


Is ChatGPT good at music theory?


ChatGPT is good at explaining music theory concepts such as scales, intervals, and chord functions. It is less reliable at multi-step music reasoning. In the 2024 MusicTheoryBench study, GPT-4 scored 58.2 percent on music knowledge and 25.6 percent on music reasoning, close to the 25 percent random baseline. Ask for note names and half steps, and check answers in a drill app.


What is the best free app to learn music theory?


musictheory.net is free with no ads, and Musicca is free, with an optional free account that removes ads. Both have lessons and graded exercises. Functional Ear Trainer is free ear-training software, and MuseScore Studio is free, open-source notation software. Pair one of them with a free AI chat tutor for explanations.


Can AI train my ear?


Yes. Adaptive ear-training apps adjust the next question to your results. EarMaster describes an intelligent questioning engine that adapts exercises to your performance, and ToneGym says its games adapt to your level. A chat tutor cannot hear you in a text chat, so use a dedicated ear trainer for intervals and chords.


Can AI generate chord progressions for my songs?


Yes. Hookpad's Aria add-on writes chords, melody, or both, and ChordChord and LANDR Composer generate progressions you can export as MIDI. A chat tutor can also suggest progressions in a key. Play each suggestion before you keep it, because the best choice depends on your melody.


Can AI teach me to play an instrument?


Apps such as Yousician, Simply Piano, flowkey, and Skoove listen to you play and give feedback on notes and timing. They teach playing, and theory comes along the way. A chat tutor explains the why behind what you play, so the two work well together.


How do I learn music theory with AI step by step?


Pair one explain tool with one check tool. Spend about 20 minutes a day: ask an AI tutor to explain one concept, write it on the staff, drill it in an ear trainer, and log the result. Move from notes and rhythm to intervals, scales, chords, progressions, and then song analysis over about 12 weeks.


How do I get accurate answers from an AI music tutor?


Ask for note names and the number of half steps, not only Roman numerals. Paste notes in one text format, such as ABC notation or a plain note list. Ask the tutor to say how sure it is. Then check the answer on a keyboard or in a free drill site such as musictheory.net.
